content: 1. Baker et al. (1989) demonstrated that oral acyclovir effectively suppresses frequent recurrences of genital herpes over a one-year period, as published in Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2. Bartlett et al. (2008) conducted the RELIEF trial, which explored famciclovir treatment options for patients experiencing frequent outbreaks of recurrent genital herpes, with findings published in the Journal of Clinical Virology. 3. Celum et al. (2008) investigated the impact of acyclovir on HIV-1 acquisition in individuals seropositive for herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) through a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, as reported in The Lancet. 4. Corey et al. (2004) evaluated the efficacy of once-daily valacyclovir in reducing the risk of genital herpes transmission, with results published in the New England Journal of Medicine. 5. Fife et al. (2007) compared one year of episodic versus suppressive treatment of recurrent genital herpes using valacyclovir, as detailed in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 6. Fife et al. (2008) conducted an international, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to assess valacyclovir's effectiveness in suppressing HSV-2 genital herpes in newly diagnosed patients, as published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 7. Fife et al. (2006) examined the effect of valacyclovir on viral shedding in immunocompetent patients with recurrent HSV-2 genital herpes through a U.S.-based randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial, with findings reported in the Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 8. Mattison et al. (1988) compared long-term suppressive therapy with short-term oral acyclovir therapy for managing recurrent genital herpes in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, as published in the American Journal of Medicine. 9. Mertz et al. (1984) conducted a multicenter, double-blind trial to evaluate the long-term suppression of frequently recurring genital herpes simplex virus infections using acyclovir, with results published in JAMA. 10. Straus et al. (1984) demonstrated the efficacy of acyclovir in suppressing frequent recurrences of genital herpes and noted a diminishing need for treatment over successive years, as reported in JAMA. 11. Mostow et al. (1988) investigated the suppression of recurrent genital herpes using single daily doses of acyclovir, with findings published in the American Journal of Medicine. 12. The International Valaciclovir HSV Study Group (1997) conducted a placebo-controlled study on the use of valacyclovir for suppressing recurrent genital HSV infections with once-daily therapy, as detailed in Genitourinary Medicine. 13. The International Valaciclovir HSV Study Group (1998) performed a large-scale dose range-finding study to evaluate valacyclovir's effectiveness in suppressing recurrent genital HSV infections, as published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. 14. Sekhin et al. (2004) assessed the efficacy of long-term suppressive therapy with valacyclovir in managing recurrent genital herpes, with findings reported in Clinical Microbiology and Infection. 15. WHO guidelines recommend suppressive therapy for genital herpes simplex virus infections, comparing the efficacy of acyclovir and valacyclovir at various dosages, based on randomized trials and systematic reviews. 16. Studies comparing suppressive famciclovir and valacyclovir regimens have shown similar efficacy in reducing HSV-2 shedding and recurrence rates, with adherence and side effects being comparable across treatment groups. 17. Suppressive therapy with antiviral drugs, such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir, has been shown to reduce genital herpes recurrences and viral shedding in both immunocompetent and HIV-infected individuals, as supported by multiple randomized controlled trials. 18. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses highlight the importance of patient adherence, cost considerations, and treatment preferences in managing recurrent genital herpes, emphasizing the role of suppressive therapy in improving quality of life and reducing transmission risk.
